newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU sends ship to sell sceptics on euro advantages.
newsitem.headline: EU sends ship to sell sceptics on euro advantages.

text.p: As European leaders fine-tuned a deal on currency union in Amsterdam, the European Commission sent a boat up the Rhine to sell a sceptical public, mainly in Germany, on the advantages of the euro.
The refitted barge, docked on Monday on the Cologne waterfront, carries a message to the grassroots that there is nothing to fear from the change to a single currency, slated for January 1999.

The floating exhibition, which set sail from Rotterdam on June 2 and will end its tour in Strasbourg in mid-July, makes its point mainly by showing that the history of money in Europe has been a process of simplifying from multiple currencies, culminating in the planned single currency, the euro.

"Before 1871, there used to be many currencies in what is now Germany but then, they were unified in the reichsmark," said Elke Vosten, an European Union educator aboard the ship. "Now, no one would say we should have a different currency in Munich than in Hamburg."

But Germans in particular remain wary of the euro, mainly because they associate the end of the deutschemark with the "currency reforms" of the past, which were thinly disguised devaluations that helped fuel hyperinflation.
A poll of 1,011 Germans released over the weekend by the Forsa research institute for RTL television found that 51 percent opposed the euro's introduction while 34 percent favoured it.
"People are afraid that they will lose what they have worked hard for all their lives, but we hope to relieve some of these fears," said Ute Halle-Block, another EU educator.

European finance ministers in Amsterdam, reflecting an increased emphasis on fighting joblessness after the Left's victory in this month's French elections, were debating on Monday how much to modify the stability pact hammered out in Dublin at the end of last year.

The stability pact is aimed at ensuring that members continue to keep a tight rein on their finances after Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) starts. But while the euro will make cross-border business easier, people say it is not a panacea.

"The euro will make things simpler, but it won't take our problems away, particularly high unemployment," said Klaus Warneke, a 40-year-old administrator, after seeing the exhibition. "It will still be cheaper to produce in Spain."
Warneke added that Germany is likely to continue to bear a disproportionate share of the costs of the single European market, as it does for the EU today.
And with Germany itself uncertain of meeting the EMU deficit target, he wondered about possible hidden consequences of loosening the criteria or delaying the start.
But most visitors appeared convinced the euro would start on time, whether or not they thought it was a good thing.
"It will happen because the efforts have been so great, but it will be shaky. That's the danger," said Nick Brisnik, a sports student.
Some visitors said they saw more advantages than disadvantages to the future system.
"It will be the same, not more or less. If I buy a car in France, I'll be able to compare the price directly," said Artur Probek, an unemployed technical draftsman.
The cafe on board posted its prices in euros as well as marks, with a 2.50 mark coffee priced at 1.28 euros. But change still came only in marks.
